data.name: Light_Brightness_P1
data.value: A lamp turns electricity into light. Double its power and twice as much light lands on the floor, yet the floor does not look twice as bright. Try it: the first few watts make a big difference, the last few hardly any.

data.name: Light_Brightness_P2
data.value: Our eyes, and the screens made for them, squeeze large amounts of light together. Keep turning it up and the floor under the lamp simply turns white: a screen cannot show anything brighter than its white.

data.name: Light_Brightness_Deeper
data.value: The picture adds light up as it really is, then bends it with the screen's curve (roughly the 1/2.2 power) just before it is shown. The chart shows that curve and where the floor under the lamp is on it.

data.name: Light_Brightness_Picture
data.value: A small lamp over a floor, with a chart of how bright the light looks

data.name: Light_Tilt_P1
data.value: Shine a torch straight down on a board, then tip the board. The beam has not changed, but it now lands on a longer patch, so every bit of the patch gets a smaller share of the light.

data.name: Light_Tilt_P2
data.value: At 60° the patch is twice as long, so it is half as bright. Tip it right over and the light just slides past. This is why sunlight warms the ground more at noon than in the evening, when it comes in low.

data.name: Light_Tilt_Deeper
data.value: Brightness = straight-on brightness × cos(angle). The patch is 1 / cos(angle) times as long.

data.name: Light_Tilt_Picture
data.value: A torch shining down on a tilting board, seen from the side

data.name: Light_Distance_P1
data.value: A small lamp sends light out in every direction. Follow just the light that passes through one square a metre away. At 2 metres that same light covers 4 such squares, at 3 metres 9.

data.name: Light_Distance_P2
data.value: Spread over more squares, each square gets less: at twice the distance, a quarter of the light. Sound from a small speaker thins out the same way.

data.name: Light_Distance_Deeper
data.value: Brightness ∝ 1 / distance². This is the inverse-square law; it holds for a lamp that is small next to the distance.

data.name: Light_Distance_Picture
data.value: A lamp and the light through one square, spreading over more squares further away

data.name: Light_Distance_Readout
data.value: The light covers {0} squares · each gets {1}%

data.name: Light_Angle_P1
data.value: A car down the road looks smaller than the same car parked next to you. What your eye takes in is not how long the car is but the angle between its two ends.

data.name: Light_Angle_P2
data.value: Draw a circle round your eye: the arc between the two lines, divided by the circle's radius, is that angle in radians. Twice as far, half the angle. For a patch instead of a line the same idea is the solid angle: how much of your view it fills.

data.name: Light_Angle_Deeper
data.value: Angle in radians = arc ÷ radius. A full turn is 2π ≈ 6.28 radians; far away, the angle ≈ size ÷ distance.

data.name: Light_Angle_Picture
data.value: From above: an eye, a car down the road and the angle between its ends

data.name: Light_Shadow_P1
data.value: A lamp hangs over a box. Stand anywhere on the floor and ask: how much of the lamp can I see past the box? Where it is all hidden, the shadow is full; where only part of it is hidden, the shadow is part dark.

data.name: Light_Shadow_P2
data.value: A small lamp is hidden all at once, so its shadow has a sharp edge. A big lamp, or a cloudy sky, is hidden a little at a time, so the edge fades gently. Raise the lamp, grow it, move it aside, and watch the edge.

data.name: Light_Shadow_Deeper
data.value: The fully dark part is the umbra, the soft edge the penumbra. The picture works out, for every point of the floor, how much of the lamp it can see.

data.name: Light_Shadow_Picture
data.value: A square lamp over a floor with a box on it

data.name: Light_Sky_Title
data.value: What a spot on the floor sees

data.name: Light_Sky_P1
data.value: Put your eye on a spot of the floor and look up: you see a half-sphere of sky. The lamp is one patch of it. Now press that half-sphere flat onto the floor, like a dome squashed into a circle: the lamp's patch lands somewhere in the circle.

data.name: Light_Sky_P2
data.value: The share of the circle the lamp covers is the share of light the spot gets. A low lamp squashes thin near the rim — that is the slant of spread 2 — and a far lamp shrinks — that is the distance of spread 3. One picture holds both.

data.name: Light_Sky_Deeper
data.value: Light received ∝ the patch's size on the sky (its solid angle) × cos(how far from overhead). Pressing the dome flat does that multiplication for you.

data.name: Light_Sky_Share
data.value: The lamp covers {0}% of the circle

data.name: Light_Sky_Picture
data.value: A spot on the floor, the half-sphere of sky over it, and a lamp pressed onto both

data.name: Light_Sky_Readout
data.value: The lamp covers {0}% of the circle: that share of a whole sky's light

data.name: Light_Radiance_Title
data.value: Why a wall looks as bright from far away

data.name: Light_Radiance_P1
data.value: Walk away from a lit wall and it does not get dimmer. Odd, since each bit of it now sends you less light. But each speck of your eye now takes in more of the wall: twice as far, four times as much wall, each part a quarter as bright to you.

data.name: Light_Radiance_P2
data.value: Turn the panel away and the same thing happens: the eye takes in more of it, and a matte surface sends less light off at a slant, by just as much. What stays the same is how bright the surface looks — its radiance — which is what eyes and cameras measure.

data.name: Light_Radiance_Deeper
data.value: Area seen ∝ distance² / cos, light from each bit ∝ cos / distance²: the product is 1. A surface that holds this at every angle is called Lambertian.

data.name: Light_Radiance_Picture
data.value: From the side: an eye's narrow cone of view meeting a glowing panel

data.name: Light_Radiance_PerBit
data.value: Light from each bit that reaches the eye: {0}×

data.name: Light_Reflection_P1
data.value: Light that lands on a surface leaves it again, but where it goes depends on the surface. A mirror sends it all on in one direction, as a ball bounces off a wall. A matte surface, like paper, scatters it every way.

data.name: Light_Reflection_P2
data.value: Most things are in between: glossy paint, a polished table. Move the eye: on a mirror you see the lamp only from one place; on paper the spot looks about the same from everywhere; on gloss you see a bright highlight that follows you.

data.name: Light_Reflection_Deeper
data.value: The shape over the surface shows how much light leaves in each direction. For a matte surface it is a circle (cos of the angle from straight up); for a mirror, a single spike at the mirror angle.

data.name: Light_Reflection_Picture
data.value: From the side: light landing on a surface and the shape of the light leaving it

data.name: Light_Bounce_P1
data.value: A red wall is red because it gives back mostly red light and keeps the rest. White gives back all colours. With no bounces, only what the lamp reaches is lit, and the box's shadow side is pitch black.

data.name: Light_Bounce_P2
data.value: Add a bounce: everything lit now lights everything else. The floor near the wall turns faintly red, and shadows fill in. A second and third bounce add less each time. This is why rooms are never as dark in the shade as the lamp alone would make them.

data.name: Light_Bounce_Deeper
data.value: Each bounce passes light between every pair of points: how much one sends, times how squarely the two face each other, over the distance squared. Computer graphics calls this radiosity, or global illumination.

data.name: Light_Bounce_Picture
data.value: A lamp over a white floor and box beside a coloured wall
